metadata.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models

problem.value: Diffusion models typically operate directly in pixel space, making optimization consume hundreds of GPU days and inference expensive.

evidence.quote: However, since these models typically operate directly in pixel space, optimization of powerful DMs often consumes hundreds of GPU days and inference is expensive due to sequential evaluations.

problem.value: High-resolution synthesis of complex scenes is computationally demanding and requires massive resources only available to a small fraction of the field.

evidence.quote: Especially high-resolution synthesis of complex, natural scenes is presently dominated by scaling up likelihood-based models, potentially containing billions of parameters in autoregressive (AR) transformers [66,67].

contributions.value: Our method scales more gracefully to higher dimensional data and can be efficiently applied to high-resolution synthesis of megapixel images.

evidence.quote: (i) In contrast to purely transformer-based approaches [23,66], our method scales more graceful to higher dimensional data and can thus (a) work on a compression level which provides more faithful and detailed reconstructions than previous work (see Fig. 1) and (b) can be efficiently Figure 2. Illustrating perceptual and semantic compression: Most bits of a digital image correspond to imperceptible details.

contributions.value: We achieve competitive performance on multiple tasks while significantly lowering computational and inference costs.

evidence.quote: (ii) We achieve competitive performance on multiple tasks (unconditional image synthesis, inpainting, stochastic super-resolution) and datasets while significantly lowering computational costs.

contributions.value: Our approach does not require a delicate weighting of reconstruction and generative abilities, ensuring faithful reconstructions and little regularization.

evidence.quote: (iii) We show that, in contrast to previous work [93] which learns both an encoder/decoder architecture and a score-based prior simultaneously, our approach does not require a delicate weighting of reconstruction and generative abilities.

contributions.value: Our model can be applied in a convolutional fashion for densely conditioned tasks to render large, consistent images.

evidence.quote: (iv) We find that for densely conditioned tasks such as super-resolution, inpainting and semantic synthesis, our model can be applied in a convolutional fashion and render large, consistent images of ∼ 1024 2 px.

contributions.value: We design a general-purpose conditioning mechanism based on cross-attention, enabling multi-modal training.

evidence.quote: (v) Moreover, we design a general-purpose conditioning mechanism based on cross-attention, enabling multi-modal training.

contributions.value: We release pretrained latent diffusion and autoencoding models that might be reusable for various tasks.

evidence.quote: (vi) Finally, we release pretrained latent diffusion and autoencoding models at https : / / github . com/CompVis/latent-diffusion which might be reusable for a various tasks besides training of DMs [81].

Our latent diffusion models (LDMs) achieve new state-of-the-art scores for image inpainting and class-conditional image synthesis and highly competitive performance on various tasks, including text-to-image synthesis, unconditional image generation and super-resolution, while significantly reducing computational requirements compared to pixel-based DMs.

method_summary.value: An autoencoder is used to compress images into a low-dimensional latent space using a perceptual loss and a patch-based adversarial objective.

evidence.quote: Our perceptual compression model is based on previous work [23] and consists of an autoencoder trained by combination of a perceptual loss [106] and a patch-based [33] adversarial objective [20,23,103].

method_summary.value: The latent space is regularized using either a KL-penalty or a vector quantization layer to avoid arbitrarily high-variance latent spaces.

evidence.quote: In order to order to avoid arbitrarily high-variance latent spaces, we experiment with two different kinds of regularizations.

method_summary.value: A diffusion model is trained in the learned latent space using a reweighted variant of the variational lower bound to predict a denoised variant.

evidence.quote: For image synthesis, the most successful models [15,30,72] rely on a reweighted variant of the variational lower bound on p(x), which mirrors denoising score-matching [85].

method_summary.value: The neural backbone of the model is a time-conditional UNet that uses cross-attention mechanisms to incorporate conditioning inputs from various modalities.

evidence.quote: The neural backbone θ (•, t) of our model is realized as a time-conditional UNet [71].

novelty.value: The approach explicitly separates the compressive learning phase from the generative learning phase.

evidence.quote: We propose to circumvent this drawback by introducing an explicit separation of the compressive from the generative learning phase (see Fig. 2).

novelty.value: Unlike previous works that used an arbitrary 1D ordering, this method preserves the 2D spatial structure of the learned latent space using mild compression rates.

evidence.quote: This is in contrast to previous works [23,66], which relied on an arbitrary 1D ordering of the learned space z to model its distribution autoregressively and thereby ignored much of the inherent structure of z.

novelty.value: Unlike previous work relying on autoregressive transformers in a discrete latent space, this approach exploits image-specific inductive biases via a UNet.

evidence.quote: Unlike previous work that relied on autoregressive, attention-based transformer models in a highly compressed, discrete latent space [23,66,103], we can take advantage of image-specific inductive biases that our model offers.

compute.value: Single NVIDIA A100 GPU used for experiments

evidence.quote: To obtain a comparable test-field, we fix the computational resources to a single NVIDIA A100 for all experiments in this section and train all models for the same number of steps and with the same number of parameters.

ablations.value: Ablation on downsampling factor f for LDM

evidence.quote: This section analyzes the behavior of our LDMs with different downsampling factors f ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32} (abbreviated as LDM-f , where LDM-1 corresponds to pixel-based DMs).

ablations.value: Ablation on first stage regularization schemes (KL vs VQ) and attention mechanisms

evidence.quote: In particular, we compare the inpainting efficiency of LDM-1 (i.e. a pixel-based conditional DM) with LDM-4, for both KL and VQ regularizations, as well as VQ-LDM-4 without any attention in the first stage (see Tab. 8), where the latter reduces GPU memory for decoding at high resolutions.

limitations.value: Sequential sampling is slower than GANs.

evidence.quote: While LDMs significantly reduce computational requirements compared to pixel-based approaches, their sequential sampling process is still slower than that of GANs.

limitations.value: Reconstruction capability can bottleneck tasks requiring fine pixel-space accuracy.

evidence.quote: Moreover, the use of LDMs can be questionable when high precision is required: although the loss of image quality is very small in our f = 4 autoencoding models (see Fig. 1), their reconstruction capability can become a bottleneck for tasks that require fine-grained accuracy in pixel space.

future_work.value: Perform a more detailed analysis of modifying the UNet architecture by conditioning on the time step.

evidence.quote: We leave a more detailed analysis of this modification to future work.

ethics.value: Generative models can facilitate the creation of manipulated data or spam.

evidence.quote: On the other hand, it also means that it becomes easier to create and disseminate manipulated data or spread misinformation and spam.
In particular, the deliberate manipulation of images ("deep fakes") is a common problem in this context, and women in particular are disproportionately affected by it [13,24].

ethics.value: Generative models can reveal sensitive training data collected without consent.

evidence.quote: Generative models can also reveal their training data [5,90], which is of great concern when the data contain sensitive or personal information and were collected without explicit consent.

ethics.value: Deep learning modules tend to reproduce or exacerbate existing data biases.

evidence.quote: Finally, deep learning modules tend to reproduce or exacerbate biases that are already present in the data [22,38,91].
